title: CRONOS: Benchmarking Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention.

extra.full_text: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cronos/

title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments.

extra.full_text: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2° on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $π_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.

title: Coordinating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Action-Conditioned Latent Foresight
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution.

extra.full_text: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Psi-Zero and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. title: Trusting Imagined Futures: Auditing Imagined Rewards for VLA Post-Training
summary: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback.

extra.full_text: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

title: Haptic Shared Control for Multi-Robot Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems offer significant advantages in terms of flexibility and redundancy, enabling the efficient distribution of complex tasks among multiple robots. However, their deployment requires advanced control strategies to ensure optimal cooperation between autonomous agents and human operators.

extra.comment: PhD thesis, Université de Rennes (IRISA UMR 6074 / Inria Rennes), defended 30 April 2025. 134 pages, 38 figures
extra.full_text: Multi-agent systems offer significant advantages in terms of flexibility and redundancy, enabling the efficient distribution of complex tasks among multiple robots. However, their deployment requires advanced control strategies to ensure optimal cooperation between autonomous agents and human operators. We propose a modification of the global connectivity maintenance algorithm to incorporate measurements taken in agent's local frame, using sensors with limited fields of view. This algorithm, responsible for the autonomous behavior of the multi-robot system, is combined with different adaptive supervision strategies, allowing the user to exert control at varying scales over the entire group. (i) Single Agent Control (S): The operator directly controls a single robot, (ii) Pinning Control (P): The operator imposes constraints on multiple robots to influence the group, (iii) Centroid Control (C): The operator acts on the system's center of mass to steer the entire fleet. In conjunction with the connectivity maintenance algorithm, these methods ensure compliance with inter-agent constraints while providing haptic feedback to the user regarding the system's connectivity state. The effectiveness of these approaches was evaluated through a user study, comparing performance with and without haptic feedback across multiple scenarios tailored to the different control modes.

title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
summary: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts.

extra.full_text: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
summary: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity.

extra.comment: For code, checkpoints and more results, check out https://arp.insait.ai
extra.full_text: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.

title: Caging Vision-Language Navigation for Legged Robots via Barrier-Certified Safety Architecture
summary: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation.

extra.full_text: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation. Therefore, this paper aims to cage Legged-Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) through a safety architecture that provides physical grounding and ensures navigation safety. The key idea is not to abandon the powerful capabilities of end-to-end VLA planning, but rather to augment and cage them. In particular, we integrate a high-level VLA planner with a low-level physical-grounding layer that leverages efficient state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and an Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation to generate executable trajectories. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function (dEBF) constraints. The proposed Legged-VLN system is modular, making it compatible with various VLM/VLA models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities.

title: Safeguarding Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Connected and Automated Vehicles with Recursively Feasible Control Barrier Functions
summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds.

extra.full_text: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.

title: WayTrace: A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy for Embodied Urban Navigation
summary: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors.

extra.full_text: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. title: GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL
summary: Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve.

extra.full_text: Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies -- typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets -- capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy's support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy's support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Project website and open-source code at https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/ .

title: SPOD: Recovering Suppressed Temporal Evidence in Video-LLMs via Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition
summary: Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have achieved strong performance on many video understanding tasks, yet remain vulnerable to temporal hallucination in time-sensitive reasoning scenarios such as scene transition understanding and event ordering.

extra.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26)
extra.full_text: Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have achieved strong performance on many video understanding tasks, yet remain vulnerable to temporal hallucination in time-sensitive reasoning scenarios such as scene transition understanding and event ordering. Existing solutions either require costly retraining or introduce inefficient multi-pass inference and external supervision at test time. In this work, we show that temporal evidence is already encoded in Video-LLM hidden representations but is not fully exploited during standard inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD), a training-free framework that recovers suppressed temporal evidence through analytical hidden-state manipulation in a single forward pass. SPOD consists of two components: Frame Distinctiveness Analysis (FDA), which identifies salient frames from middle-layer hidden-state geometry, and Temporal Delta Subspace (TDS), which constructs orthogonal temporal and prior subspaces from weighted inter-frame hidden-state differences. By decomposing final hidden states into temporal, prior, and residual components and rescaling them independently, SPOD enhances dynamic information, suppresses static appearance bias, and preserves complementary information. Experiments on VidHalluc, EventHallusion, and VideoMMMU show that SPOD consistently outperforms strong inference-time baselines across temporal reasoning tasks and model architectures while retaining near-vanilla inference efficiency. These results suggest that improving temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs may depend not only on additional supervision, but also on recovering temporal evidence already present in their internal representations. Our code is available at https://github.com/VioAgnes/SPOD.

title: Are Drone Ports the Next Annoying Tech Neighbor?
summary: Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September.

extra.full_text: Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September. The noise had them spending less time outside in their garden, and even inside their home, they couldn’t escape the near-constant buzzing. Angry and feeling harassed, the LeComptes began to think about moving. The problem: delivery drones. Amazon’s MK30 delivery drones are large and must fly near the ground when making deliveries. Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association/AP Images Last August, Amazon Prime Air began flying its MK30 drones from a distribution center 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from the LeComptes’ home. People in the neighborhood first noticed just a few of the drones, flying high (U.S. regulations authorize drones to fly at up to 120 meters (400 feet )). But a couple of weeks later, they felt as if drones were everywhere, and often flying much lower. The high-pitched whine of rotors was what bothered them the most, says Blake Fugler, who lives in the same neighborhood. It sounded as if a neighbor was constantly using a weed whacker for hours every day, he says. Acoustic research has found that the noise of drone rotors is more annoying than that of cars, airplanes, and other familiar background sounds. Once flights became frequent, the noise made people miserable. “Outside the house on a Saturday between 9 and 10 a.m., I counted a drone every 48 seconds,” says Fugler’s partner, Cristina Boone. Delivery Drone Concerns Neighbors had concerns about drones buzzing over playgrounds, schools, and services at the local cemetery; a drone that made a forced landing on the median of a busy highway; and the fact that drones are equipped with cameras. Then word spread about Amazon’s plans as reported in the FAA’s Environmental Assessment for the facility : “Operations would occur between 6 a.m. and 10:30 p.m., with 100 of the 1,000 daily delivery operations (10%) occurring during the period from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.” As they quickly expand their operations around the world, delivery-drone companies -- including Amazon Prime Air , Alphabet’s Wing Aviation , Zipline , Manna Aero , Doordash Air , Matternet , Meituan , JD Logistics , and more, say their flying robots are quiet , safe , and unobtrusive . Massive expansion is planned for the near future. In Asia, for example, Meituan launched its latest “low-altitude delivery network’’ in September in Shanghai , while JD continues to expand drone service in rural China . In the U.S., Zipline and Uber have announced a partnership with the goal of 1 million drone deliveries a day by the end of 2029. Wing aims to have 270 U.S. drone hubs operating by the end of 2027 . And Amazon Prime Air, which currently delivers in about 85 municipalities in the U.S., says it plans to serve 500 by the end of 2026. A Wing “nest” of delivery drones in a parking lot. Wing Yet as the companies aggressively scale up, “the public outreach piece has probably been more of an afterthought than it should have been,” says David Ison , a specialist in Emerging Aviation Technologies and Land Use Compatibility at the Washington State Department of Transportation, who has worked on the state’s drone-hub land-use guidelines. “I think what companies assumed is everybody would be cheering that they could get things delivered by drone in half an hour.” Companies tout drone delivery as a way to do good. Zipline has delivered blood plasma and vaccines in Africa . Material that Wing provided at public meetings in the Dallas Fort Worth area says its deliveries there have saved more than 1,000 tonnes of carbon that would have been emitted by delivery trucks. For businesses, drone delivery is supposed to offer faster service and reduce costs, although whether drones are actually less costly is a complex question that depends on a variety of interconnected factors . The commercial and philanthropic use cases make for an unusual sales pitch, notes Ison. “It’s a lot easier argument to make when you’re saying you’re delivering blood to an accident site than when you’re delivering a fidget toy.” But instead of being impressed, people troubled by drones say they feel they’re being pushed around by a distant corporation. “It’s the same way data centers strong-arm communities,” says Boone. Newly arrived drone launch sites have triggered similar fears from China to France to Australia to within many communities in the United States, including suburban Detroit , Richardson, Texas , Glendale, Ariz ., East Cobb, Ga ., Maplewood, Mo ., and Westborough, Mass . The response has sometimes been enough to shut down local drone operations completely. An early Wing trial in 2018 in suburban Canberra, Australia, shut down a few months later, after activists formed an opposition group and rallied support in Parliament . In response, the company “fundamentally reshaped our engineering priorities, flight operations, and community-engagement strategy,” says Jessie Poole-Strang, Wing’s communications lead. It redesigned its drones to reduce noise, changed flight-path algorithms, and now makes efforts to familiarize people with its robots before a facility opens. Communities Take Action Still, legal and political campaigns against drones continue to arise. On 28 September, 15 U.S. states and Harris County, Texas, sued the FAA to stop it from easing its environmental assessment rules for drone sites, which are key to local government control. In April, the Cobb County Board of Commissioners in Georgia denied a zoning request for a Wing drone facility there. In response to the Cobb County complaints, a Wing spokesperson said the company was hearing “positive feedback” from people in Cobb County. Similarly, Amazon representatives have said most feedback from customers about drone delivery is “ overwhelmingly positive ,” and Zipline has encouraged at least one local official to refer to drone delivery as a “totally normal part of life.” Wing’s drone is smaller and lighter than some other delivery drones. Wing But fundamental concerns remain. “There are safety, noise, and visual-pollution issues with all these platforms,” Ison says, noting that it’s important not to lump all drone technologies together. For example, concerns about accidents are more relevant to Amazon’s MK-30 drone, which weighs almost 36 kilograms (80 pounds) , than to Wing’s largest drone, which weighs less than 11 kilograms (25 pounds) with its payload included . Another safety consideration: Wing and Zipline , he notes, lower their packages to the ground via a tether, which leaves the craft higher in the air than Amazon’s , which must get low enough to drop its load without damage. And Ison expects continuing disputes about noise. This is because U.S. law is not settled on people’s rights to airspace just above their property. “Maybe someone says, ‘You can’t fly over my house’ or ‘I want you to pay me to fly over my house,’ ” Ison says. “That is a murky area that is going to have to be worked out in court.” For now, in the Baton Rouge neighborhood where the LeComptes, Fugler, and Boone live, the skies have calmed. Their councilman says Amazon Prime Air has responded to the outcry by rerouting 70 percent of drone flights elsewhere, although since the drones are not allowed to fly over highways, that likely means other residential neighborhoods. As of late October, LeCompte says she is now seeing, “two or three a day” over their home, although on a trip to the bank a few miles away, she counted eight in 20 minutes. “Sorry for those folks, but I thank Amazon for clearing our sky.”
